items.title: Louie Bellson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: the first couple weeks Billy Strayhorn and I roomed together, because he used to go with the band once in a while.

ctx.x: We were talking about your time with Duke’s band. Obviously he felt comfortable enough with you and either invited you or allowed you to bring your own music. Can you talk about how that process came about?

When Tizol came to me after I’d been in the band a couple of months – the first couple weeks Billy Strayhorn and I roomed together, because he used to go with the band once in a while. There’s a genius. Billy Strayhorn was a genius. I learned an awful lot. I made the mistake of saying to him, when I first met him, “Strayhorn, how did Duke voice Caravan?” He went like this to me: naaaaaaaaa. They kept their ideas secret. Only later on, they came to me, and Duke showed me how they did it. But when I first joined…
The thing that knocked me out with, the first time he heard The Hawk Talks, he recorded it on Columbia. I was amazed.

items.title: Louie Bellson interviewed by Monk Rowe, Sarasota, Florida, April 12, 1996
items.q: They had Strayhorn and Duke and Clark Terry stay in one house, and Carney and Russell Procope and myself in another house

ctx.x: Something to learn from Basie. Getting back to Ellington for a moment, did you get a chance to see Ellington and Strayhorn, how they collaborated on their music? It seems like such a fascinating thing the way they pulled that off.

Well you know Ellington — I mean Strayhorn joined Ellington as a lyricist and from what I hear and Billy Strayhorn told me that I don’t think that Duke knew at first that he arranged as a lyricist. So Duke gave Strayhorn an assignment for lyrics, and he said “I’ll check you out when I get back, we’ve got to go to Europe.” So when they came back from Europe, Billy said “I write arrangements also.” So Duke said “really?” He said “do you have one?” He said “yeah.” And that was “Take the A Train.” And I think…

items.title: Louie Bellson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: If Duke would get an idea, he’d say, “Strays” – we used to call him Strays – “Strays, do this.” Strays would pick up from him and continue.

ctx.x: What was that dynamic like? Was there much talking? What was it like?
Not too much talking. If Duke would get an idea, he’d say, “Strays” – we used to call him Strays – “Strays, do this.” Strays would pick up from him and continue. No
dialogue. It was almost like they knew which way they were going before they did it. That’s unbelievable, but that’s true.
